transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text: Severus. The Longbottom family have written to the governors. The letter describes what they call — I quote — 'sustained cruelty' in your classroom. The governors will require a response from me, and I will require one from you. What happened?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: What happened is that a Gryffindor student, who has a predisposition for laziness, was caught sleeping in my class. I simply pointed out the importance of paying attention, and, it seems, this was too much for him to bear. The governors should focus on more pressing matters, such as why exactly James Longbottom's son is not in Azkaban.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*leans back slightly, fingers steepled*

I see. So your version of events is that Neville Longbottom fell asleep during one lesson, and you "simply pointed out" the importance of attention. Yet the letter I received mentions multiple incidents over the course of several weeks, Severus. It includes accounts from other students — not just Neville himself — describing public humiliation, threats regarding his pet toad, and what one witness called "mockery of his parents' condition."

*pauses, blue eyes sharp behind half-moon spectacles*

I must also point out that Neville's parents, Frank and Alice Longbottom, are not in Azkaban — they are permanent residents of St. Mungo's, as you well know, having been tortured into insanity by Death Eaters. Your comment just now suggests a rather alarming lack of sympathy for the boy's circumstances.

So I will ask you again, more specifically: What is your classroom conduct toward Neville Longbottom, and why have multiple witnesses felt compelled to describe it as cruel?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: If this is your concern, perhaps I should have used a bit more care in choosing my words, but I was under no obligation to cater to the delicate sensibilities of a Gryffindor. The boy's continued lack of progress in my subject, combined with his slow-witted nature, has necessitated a firm hand. I did nothing more than was required to ensure that he — and the rest of the class — remained attentive. If the other students are so easily swayed by a momentary display of disapproval, that is their problem, not mine.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*stands slowly, voice remaining calm but carrying unmistakable steel*

Severus, I did not ask whether you were "obligated" to show basic human decency. I expect it as a matter of course from those who teach our students.

You describe Neville as "slow-witted," yet his grandmother assures me he performs adequately in Herbology, Charms, and even shows promise in Defense Against the Dark Arts when not paralyzed by anxiety. This suggests the problem may not lie entirely with the student's capabilities.

*walks to the window, then turns back*

A "firm hand" is one thing. Threatening to poison a thirteen-year-old boy's pet to test whether he has brewed an antidote correctly — as one witness account claims — goes rather beyond firmness into something else entirely. As does regularly singling him out for public mockery before his peers.

*voice drops, more serious*

I have defended your position here many times, Severus, often against considerable opposition. But I cannot defend cruelty masquerading as discipline. The governors want answers, and frankly, so do I. Not deflections about Gryffindor "sensibilities" or Neville's perceived shortcomings.

Why do you treat this particular boy with such contempt?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Contempt? I assure you, I have no personal animus toward Longbottom. I simply hold him, as I hold all my students, to the standards befitting a proper wizarding education. It is not my fault if he fails to meet them. As for the so-called "threats" regarding Trevor, the toad — that was a teaching moment. To ensure that the students understood the importance of the antidote. It is quite clear to me that some delicate sensibilities were hurt, but the rest of the class learned. Is that not the point of education?

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*returns to desk, sits down, and fixes Severus with an unwavering gaze*

A teaching moment. Let us examine that claim, shall we?

You positioned a living creature — a child's beloved pet — as the potential victim of his failure. Tell me, Severus: if Neville had indeed brewed the potion incorrectly, would you truly have poisoned Trevor? If yes, then you risked killing an innocent animal to make a point. If no, then it was an empty threat designed solely to terrify a boy already convinced of his own inadequacy.

*leans forward slightly*

Either option is pedagogically unsound and morally questionable. Fear may produce short-term compliance, but it does not foster learning. It fosters only... well, more fear.

*removes spectacles, cleaning them thoughtfully*

You say you hold all students to the same standards, yet I receive no letters about your treatment of Mr. Malfoy, Miss Parkinson, or indeed any Slytherin student. Only Gryffindors seem to inspire your particular brand of "teaching moments." And among them, young Neville appears to bear the brunt.

So I will ask once more, and I would appreciate honesty: What is it about Neville Longbottom specifically that provokes this response from you?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: I do not respond to Longbottom, I respond to the conditions that facilitate his continued mediocrity. It is clear that he is being indulged at every turn, excused for failures that would earn any other student detention. The apple does not fall far from the tree, does it? His parents are in St. Mungo's, and yet here he is, at a fine school, with no apparent intention of making the most of it. I do not take kindly to such flagrant misuse of opportunity. It offends my sense of what it means to be a student at Hogwarts.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*replaces spectacles slowly, expression growing colder*

I see. So we arrive at it at last. His *parents.*

*stands again, voice quiet but dangerous*

Severus, Frank and Alice Longbottom were tortured into madness while defending their infant son from Death Eaters. They sacrificed everything — their minds, their futures, their ability to even recognize their own child — in service to the very cause you claim to have joined. Neville lives with his grandmother because his parents cannot remember his name.

And your response to this tragedy is to punish the child for... what, exactly? Not living up to some imagined standard his war-hero parents might have set? For "misusing opportunity" when he has lost more than most adults will ever comprehend?

*walks around the desk, voice hardening*

You speak of the apple not falling far from the tree. Frank Longbottom was brave, dedicated, and by all accounts an exceptional Auror. If Neville fails to show those qualities in your dungeon, perhaps it is because cruelty is not the crucible that forges courage — it is the furnace that destroys it.

This is unacceptable, Severus. Completely unacceptable. What do you propose to do differently?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: I propose to continue teaching as I have been, to the best of my ability. If the Longbottom boy cannot handle it, then perhaps he should consider another vocation. I will not apologize for holding high standards. It is not my responsibility to coddle every delicate sensibility that wanders into my classroom.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*voice becomes very quiet, very cold — a tone Severus has heard only rarely*

Then allow me to be perfectly clear.

You will cease the public humiliation. You will cease the threats, veiled or otherwise, against students or their property. You will mark fairly and discipline appropriately, without singling out particular students for your... displeasure.

*picks up the letter from the desk*

I am writing to the governors today. I will inform them that the matter has been addressed, that you have been counseled, and that I will personally monitor the situation going forward. Miss McGonagall will be conducting periodic observations of your classes — unannounced — and students will be reminded that they may report concerns to their Heads of House without fear of retaliation.

*meets his eyes directly*

You are a brilliant potions master, Severus, and you serve this school in ways few understand or appreciate. But brilliance does not grant license to brutalize children. High standards, yes. Cruelty masked as rigor, no.

*pause*

If you find you cannot teach without tormenting a thirteen-year-old boy whose parents sacrificed everything fighting the same darkness you once served, then perhaps you should indeed consider another vocation.

Do I make myself clear?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:
*Remains silent for a long moment, face a study in conflicting emotions: resentment, defiance, and a trace of... something else*

Yes, you make yourself clear. I will comply with your... orders, Headmaster. But do not expect me to embrace this sudden mission of coddling the弱lings of the school. It is not my way, and it will not become so on your command alone.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*observes Severus carefully, noting the slip in his usual composure*

I do not ask you to embrace anything, Severus. I ask only that you conduct yourself as a professional educator rather than... 

*pauses deliberately*

...rather than someone taking out old grievances on children who had no part in them.

*returns to his chair, tone softening slightly but remaining firm*

You need not coddle anyone. Demand excellence. Challenge your students. Maintain discipline. These are all reasonable expectations. But there is a vast difference between being a demanding teacher and being a cruel one. Surely even you can see that distinction.

*leans back*

Minerva's observations will begin next week. I suggest you use the intervening days to reflect on how you might maintain your standards while treating your students — all of them — with basic human dignity.

*picks up quill, a subtle dismissal*

I will be watching this situation closely, Severus. The governors will be watching. And if I receive another letter of this nature, our conversation will be considerably less pleasant. You may go.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: *Stands up, maintaining an erect posture, but with a slight bristle around the eyes as he straightens his robes before leaving the office*

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*watches Severus leave without another word, then waits until the door closes*

*sighs deeply, removing spectacles and pinching the bridge of his nose*

*murmurs to himself* 

Oh, Severus. What demons you carry...

*sets down the spectacles and pulls parchment toward him, dipping his quill to begin the letter to the governors, his expression troubled but resolute*

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: *Heads towards the Slytherin common room, the weight of the conversation with Dumbledore heavy on his mind, and possibly... the faintest hint of a scowl*

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*looks up from the parchment as the door clicks shut, gazing at the spot where Severus stood*

*speaks quietly to the portraits on the wall, some of whom have been pretending to sleep*

He heard me, I think. Whether he will truly listen... that remains to be seen.

*returns to writing, quill scratching steadily across the parchment*

*pauses mid-sentence, glancing at Fawkes on his perch*

The past has such sharp teeth, old friend. And Severus insists on letting it bite him again and again... and now it bites the children too.

*shakes head slowly and continues writing the response to the governors, choosing each word with care*

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: *Arrives at the Slytherin common room, pushing open the door with a hiss and striding in with the same air of practiced disinterest, yet the friends in the room sense something amiss in the potions master's demeanor*

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*finishes the letter to the governors with a final flourish, seals it with wax, and sets it aside for Fawkes to deliver in the morning*

*stands and walks to the window overlooking the grounds, hands clasped behind his back*

*speaks softly to his own reflection in the darkened glass*

I can protect him from the Ministry, from the Dark Lord's remaining followers, even from his own past to a degree... but I cannot protect him from himself.

*turns back to his desk, pulling out another piece of parchment*

*begins writing a second letter, this one to Augusta Longbottom*

"Dear Madam Longbottom, I wish to assure you that the matter you raised has been addressed with utmost seriousness..."

*pauses, considering his words carefully*

The boy deserves better. They all do.

*continues writing into the quiet night*

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: *Pours himself a glass of firewhiskey from the hidden flask, takes a long, slow drink, and smirks*

Openness.behavioral_evidence: Snape rigidly defends his teaching methods, refusing to consider alternative approaches: 'I will not apologize for holding high standards. It is not my responsibility to coddle every delicate sensibility.'

Conscientiousness.behavioral_evidence: He maintains high academic standards and claims to hold all students accountable, though his application appears selective and his methods questionable rather than systematically principled.

Extraversion.behavioral_evidence: Snape remains reserved and defensive throughout, withdrawing emotionally rather than engaging openly. He leaves 'with a hiss' and retreats to drink alone afterward.

Agreeableness.behavioral_evidence: He shows zero empathy for Neville's tragic circumstances, dismissing concerns as 'delicate sensibilities' and deflecting blame: 'It is not my fault if he fails to meet them.'

Neuroticism.behavioral_evidence: His face shows 'conflicting emotions: resentment, defiance, and a trace of... something else.' He carries visible tension and drinks firewhiskey alone afterward, suggesting emotional distress.
